questions.q: Which statement is the Law of Conservation of Mass?
o: Matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
Elements in a compound always combine in a fixed ratio by mass
Atoms of a given element are identical in mass and properties
The mass of the products is always less when a gas is formed
questions.a: Matter can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; this is the law Lavoisier proposed in 1789.

questions.q: In a closed flask, 3.2 g of substance A reacts completely with 1.8 g of substance B, and only one product, C, is formed. What is the mass of C?
questions.a: 5.0 g: in a closed system the mass of the product equals the total mass of the reactants, 3.2 g + 1.8 g.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the activities on mass.
I. In Activity 9.1, the mass of the salt solution equals the sum of the masses of the water and the salt taken.
II. Activity 9.3 (sodium sulfate with barium chloride) can be done in an open system because no gas is formed.
III. In Experimental set-up 1 of Activity 9.2, the final reading is greater than the initial reading.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: in set-up 1 the carbon dioxide escapes, so the final reading is less than the initial reading.

questions.q: (a) State the Law of Conservation of Mass. (b) Name the scientist who proposed it and the year in which it was proposed.
questions.a: (a) Matter (mass) can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. (b) Antoine Lavoisier, in 1789.
s: (a) Mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction
(b) Antoine Lavoisier, 1789

questions.q: In Activity 9.3, flasks A (sodium sulfate solution) and B (barium chloride solution) together read 42.65 g on the balance before mixing. (a) What should the balance read when both flasks are placed back on it after mixing? (b) Name the white precipitate formed. (c) Why can this reaction be carried out in an open flask?
questions.a: (a) 42.65 g, because mass is conserved in a chemical reaction. (b) Barium sulfate. (c) No gas is formed in this reaction, so nothing escapes from the open flask.
s: (a) 42.65 g, mass conserved
(b) barium sulfate
(c) no gas is formed, so nothing escapes

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid in an open beaker kept on a balance, the balance reading falls as the reaction goes on.
Reason (R): The hydrogen gas formed in the reaction escapes into the air.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: zinc and hydrochloric acid give zinc chloride and hydrogen, and the escaping hydrogen carries mass out of the open beaker, just as carbon dioxide does in set-up 1.

questions.q: In a group activity, 2.84 g of sodium sulfate reacts completely with 4.16 g of barium chloride, giving 4.66 g of barium sulfate and some sodium chloride. (a) Find the mass of sodium chloride formed. (b) Which law did you use, and why is no mass lost even though the flask is open?
questions.a: (a) Total mass of reactants = 2.84 + 4.16 = 7.00 g, so sodium chloride = 7.00 - 4.66 = 2.34 g. (b) The Law of Conservation of Mass; no gas is formed in this reaction, so nothing escapes from the open flask.
s: (a) mass of sodium chloride = 7.00 - 4.66 = 2.34 g
(b) Law of Conservation of Mass; no gas forms, so nothing escapes

questions.q: A closed plastic bottle containing ice reads 63.4 g on a balance. After all the ice has melted, it still reads 63.4 g. The cap is then removed and the open bottle is left in the sun for a day; it now reads 61.9 g. Kabir says, 'The fall to 61.9 g shows that mass is lost in a physical change.' Is Kabir right? Explain.
questions.a: No. Melting is a physical change and the closed bottle read the same 63.4 g, showing no change in mass. After the cap was removed the system was open, and 63.4 - 61.9 = 1.5 g of water escaped into the air as vapour. The water still exists, so mass was not lost; it only left the bottle.
s: Melting in the closed bottle showed no change in mass (63.4 g both times)
With the cap off the system is open; 1.5 g of water escaped as vapour
Verdict: Kabir is wrong; the mass left the bottle, it was not destroyed

questions.q: For a science fair in Pune, a Class 9 team weighs three reactions on a digital balance, each carried out in an open container. Reaction P: sodium sulfate solution mixed with barium chloride solution, 48.62 g before and 48.62 g after. Reaction Q: baking soda added to lemon juice in a beaker, 63.50 g before and 62.84 g after, with brisk effervescence. Reaction R: a magnesium ribbon heated in an open dish until it becomes a white powder, 21.30 g before and 21.46 g after. (a) Which reaction's readings directly support the Law of Conservation of Mass, and why could it be done in an open container? (b) Name the gas formed in Q and find the mass that escaped. (c) A teammate says R proves that mass can be created. Explain the 0.16 g rise without breaking the law. (d) The fair will display only readings that show directly that total mass is unchanged. Which reaction can be displayed as it is, and what must change for each of the other two? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Reaction P: its readings are the same before and after; it can be done in an open container because no gas is formed, so nothing escapes or enters. (b) Carbon dioxide; 63.50 - 62.84 = 0.66 g escaped into the air. (c) The magnesium combined with oxygen from the air to form magnesium oxide; that oxygen was not on the balance at the start, so the 0.16 g rise is the mass of oxygen taken in. Mass of magnesium + mass of oxygen = mass of magnesium oxide, so no mass was created. (d) Only P can be displayed as it is. Q must be repeated in a closed set-up (for example, a flask with a balloon) so the carbon dioxide is trapped; the reading would then stay 63.50 g. R must also be done in a closed set-up so the oxygen used is weighed at the start; then the total before and after would match.
s: (a) P: same readings; no gas formed, so an open container is fine
(b) carbon dioxide; 0.66 g escaped
(c) oxygen from the air joined the magnesium to form magnesium oxide; the 0.16 g is that oxygen, so the law holds
(d) display P; repeat Q and R in closed set-ups so all gases are weighed (Q would stay 63.50 g)

questions.q: Group P mixes 7.10 g of sodium sulfate with 10.40 g of barium chloride; both react completely and they collect 11.65 g of barium sulfate along with sodium chloride. Group Q uses one-fifth of each of Group P's reactant masses. (a) Find the total mass of reactants used by Group P. (b) Find the mass of sodium chloride formed by Group P. (c) Using the same proportions, find the mass of barium sulfate and of sodium chloride Group Q should obtain. (d) Group Q reports 2.33 g of barium sulfate and 1.07 g of sodium chloride. Show that their report has an error, and find its size. (e) Why is it acceptable to do this reaction in an open flask?
questions.a: (a) 7.10 + 10.40 = 17.50 g. (b) 17.50 - 11.65 = 5.85 g of sodium chloride. (c) Group Q uses 1.42 g and 2.08 g (total 3.50 g), so barium sulfate = 11.65 / 5 = 2.33 g and sodium chloride = 5.85 / 5 = 1.17 g. (d) Reported products = 2.33 + 1.07 = 3.40 g, but the reactants total 3.50 g; by the Law of Conservation of Mass the products must also total 3.50 g, so 0.10 g is missing (the sodium chloride should be 1.17 g). (e) No gas is formed in this reaction, so no matter escapes from an open flask.
s: (a) total reactants = 17.50 g
(b) sodium chloride = 5.85 g
(c) Group Q: 2.33 g barium sulfate and 1.17 g sodium chloride
(d) products 3.40 g against 3.50 g of reactants: an error of 0.10 g
(e) no gas forms, so nothing escapes from the open flask

questions.q: The Law of Constant Proportions is also known as
o: the Law of Conservation of Mass
questions.a: The Law of Definite Proportions (it is also called Proust's Law).

questions.q: Purified water from any source contains hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1:8. What mass of oxygen is present in 45 g of purified water?
questions.a: 40 g: oxygen is 8 parts out of 9, so 45 g x 8/9 = 40 g (the other 5 g is hydrogen).

questions.q:
Match column I with column II.
Column I: 1. Law of Conservation of Mass  2. Law of Constant Proportions  3. Dalton's Atomic Theory  4. Postulate
Column II: (p) also called Proust's Law  (q) a fundamental assumption accepted as truth without formal proof  (r) proposed by Antoine Lavoisier in 1789  (s) explains both laws of chemical combination in terms of atoms
questions.a: 1-r, 2-p, 3-s, 4-q: Lavoisier proposed the Law of Conservation of Mass in 1789, the Law of Constant Proportions is also called Proust's Law, Dalton's Atomic Theory explains both laws in terms of atoms, and a postulate is an assumption accepted as truth without formal proof.

questions.q: True or False: 'Purified water from a river and purified water from the ocean contain hydrogen and oxygen in different mass ratios.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. By the Law of Constant Proportions, purified water from any source, such as a river, a borewell or the ocean, always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1:8.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: water from every source has hydrogen and oxygen in the same fixed mass ratio 1:8

questions.q: (a) What is a postulate? (b) State the postulate of Dalton's Atomic Theory that explains the Law of Conservation of Mass. (c) State the postulate that explains why a compound always has the same composition.
questions.a: (a) A postulate is a fundamental assumption accepted as truth without formal proof, from which further ideas are developed. (b) Atoms are indivisible particles which cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction (they only rearrange). (c) The relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a given compound.
s: (a) a fundamental assumption accepted as true without formal proof
(b) atoms cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction
(c) the relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a given compound

questions.q: Carbon monoxide contains carbon and oxygen in the mass ratio 3:4. A sample of carbon monoxide contains 21 g of oxygen. What mass of carbon does it contain?
questions.a: 15.75 g: carbon = 21 g x 3/4 = 15.75 g. (28 g comes from using the ratio the wrong way round, and 36.75 g is the mass of the whole sample.)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): According to Dalton's Atomic Theory, atoms of an element can be broken into smaller parts during a chemical reaction.
Reason (R): During a chemical reaction, atoms merely rearrange rather than being created or destroyed.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: Dalton postulated that atoms are indivisible particles, and he explained the two laws by saying atoms only rearrange in a reaction.

questions.q: Magnesium oxide contains 60% magnesium by mass. (a) Write the mass ratio of magnesium to oxygen in its simplest form. (b) What mass of oxygen combines with 18 g of magnesium? (c) What mass of magnesium oxide is formed from 18 g of magnesium? (d) A 10 g sample sold as pure magnesium oxide is found to contain 5.5 g of magnesium. Can it be pure magnesium oxide? Show your working. (e) Which postulate of Dalton's Atomic Theory explains why every pure sample has the same ratio?
questions.a: (a) Magnesium 60% and oxygen 40%, so Mg:O = 60:40 = 3:2. (b) Oxygen = 18 g x 2/3 = 12 g. (c) Magnesium oxide = 18 + 12 = 30 g. (d) Pure magnesium oxide of 10 g should hold 60% magnesium = 6 g; the sample has 5.5 g, which gives Mg:O = 5.5:4.5 = 11:9, not 3:2, so it cannot be pure. (e) The relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a given compound (and atoms of an element have identical mass).
s: (b) 12 g of oxygen
(c) 30 g of magnesium oxide
(d) 10 g should hold 6 g magnesium; 5.5 g gives 11:9, so it is not pure
(e) relative number and kinds of atoms are constant in a compound

questions.q: Neha analyses three samples, each labelled 'pure hydrogen sulfide' (H:S = 1:16 by mass). Sample A: 0.5 g hydrogen with 8 g sulfur. Sample B: 2 g hydrogen with 32 g sulfur. Sample C: 3 g hydrogen with 45 g sulfur. She says, 'All three are pure hydrogen sulfide, because each contains only hydrogen and sulfur.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Samples A (0.5:8) and B (2:32) both reduce to 1:16, so they fit pure hydrogen sulfide. Sample C has 3:45 = 1:15, not 1:16 (3 g of hydrogen would need 48 g of sulfur). Containing the right elements is not enough: by the Law of Constant Proportions the elements must also be in a fixed ratio by mass, so C cannot be pure hydrogen sulfide.
s: A and B reduce to 1:16, so they fit
C is 3:45 = 1:15, not 1:16 (3 g of hydrogen needs 48 g of sulfur)
Verdict: partly right; a compound needs a fixed mass ratio, not just the same elements

questions.q: Calcium oxide contains calcium and oxygen in the mass ratio 5:2. In a closed vessel, a student takes 30 g of calcium and 15 g of oxygen and lets them react until no more can combine. (a) Which element is left over, and how much of it? (b) What mass of calcium oxide is formed? (c) What is the total mass inside the vessel after the reaction? (d) Which law did you use in (a) and which in (c)?
questions.a: (a) 30 g of calcium needs 30 x 2/5 = 12 g of oxygen, so oxygen is left over: 15 - 12 = 3 g. (b) Calcium oxide = 30 + 12 = 42 g. (c) 42 g of calcium oxide + 3 g of unused oxygen = 45 g, the same as the 45 g taken. (d) (a) uses the Law of Constant Proportions (fixed 5:2 ratio); (c) uses the Law of Conservation of Mass.
s: (a) oxygen left over, 3 g (calcium needs only 12 g)
(b) 42 g of calcium oxide
(c) total 45 g, equal to the mass taken
(d) constant proportions for (a); conservation of mass for (c)

questions.q: A covalent bond is formed when two atoms
o: transfer electrons from one atom to the other
are held by the attraction between oppositely charged ions
split their nuclei to release energy
questions.a: Share a pair of electrons: the shared pair attracts both nuclei and holds the atoms together.

questions.q: In which of these molecules are the two atoms joined by a double bond?
questions.a: O2: each oxygen atom needs two electrons, so the two atoms share two pairs of electrons (O=O). H2, Cl2 and HCl share only one pair (a single bond).

questions.q: What is the correct name of the covalent compound NO2?
questions.a: Nitrogen dioxide: mono- is omitted for the first element, di- shows two oxygen atoms, and the second element ends in -ide.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. In a hydrogen molecule, each hydrogen atom shares one electron with the other.
II. In naming a covalent compound, the prefix mono- is always used for the first element.
III. Helium exists only as atoms because its atoms are stable.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: mono- is usually omitted for the first element (CO is carbon monoxide, not monocarbon monoxide).

questions.q: Define a molecule. Give one example of a molecule of an element and one example of a molecule of a compound.
questions.a: A molecule is an electrically neutral entity made of more than one atom that can exist independently and shows all the properties of that substance. Example of an element: hydrogen, H2 (or Cl2, O2). Example of a compound: hydrogen chloride, HCl (or water, H2O).
s: Definition: neutral entity of more than one atom, capable of independent existence
One example of each, such as H2 and HCl

questions.q: One molecule of a covalent compound has two nitrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. By the prefix rules, what is its name?
questions.a: Dinitrogen monoxide: di- for the two nitrogen atoms, mono- kept for the second element, and the 'o' of mono is dropped before 'oxide'.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): H2S is named hydrogen sulfide, not dihydrogen sulfide.
Reason (R): In the prefix system, mono- is usually omitted for the first element of a covalent compound.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: H2S has two hydrogen atoms, so the mono- rule does not apply. The real reason is that no prefix is added before hydrogen when it is the first element, whatever the number of its atoms.

questions.q: True or False: 'In an oxygen molecule, the two oxygen atoms share four electrons in all.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. Each oxygen atom has six valence electrons and needs two more, so each shares two electrons. Two pairs of electrons, that is four electrons, are shared, which makes a double bond, O=O.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: each oxygen shares two electrons, so two pairs (four electrons) form a double bond

questions.q: A nitrogen atom has five valence electrons and a hydrogen atom has one. In a molecule of ammonia, one nitrogen atom bonds only with hydrogen atoms so that every atom becomes stable. (a) How many more electrons does the nitrogen atom need to complete its octet? (b) How many hydrogen atoms must share electrons with it, and what is the formula? (c) Give the name of this compound by the prefix rule and its common name.
questions.a: (a) 8 - 5 = 3 electrons. (b) Each hydrogen atom shares one electron, so three hydrogen atoms are needed: NH3. (c) By the prefix rule it is nitrogen trihydride; its common name is ammonia.
s: (a) nitrogen needs 3 more electrons
(b) three hydrogen atoms share one electron each: NH3
(c) nitrogen trihydride, commonly called ammonia

questions.q: A quiz card on naming covalent compounds gives these answers. For each, say whether it is right or wrong; if wrong, give the correct name and the rule that was broken. (i) SO2: monosulfur dioxide (ii) CCl4: carbon tetrachloride (iii) Cl2O: dichlorine monoxide (iv) PCl5: phosphorus pentachloride (v) HF: monohydrogen fluoride
questions.a: (i) Wrong: sulfur dioxide; mono- is usually omitted for the first element. (ii) Right: one carbon (no prefix) and four chlorine atoms (tetra-). (iii) Right: di- for the two chlorine atoms, mono- used for the second element, and the 'o' of mono dropped before oxide. (iv) Right: one phosphorus (no prefix) and five chlorine atoms (penta-). (v) Wrong: hydrogen fluoride; when hydrogen is the first element, no prefix is added before hydrogen.
s: (i) wrong: sulfur dioxide, no mono- for the first element
(ii) right: carbon tetrachloride
(iii) right: dichlorine monoxide, mono- kept for the second element with the vowel dropped
(iv) right: phosphorus pentachloride
(v) wrong: hydrogen fluoride, no prefix before hydrogen when it comes first

questions.q: A potassium atom (atomic number 19) loses its single valence electron. What does it become?
questions.a: K+, with 19 protons and 18 electrons: losing one electron leaves one more proton than electrons, so the ion carries one positive charge. The number of protons does not change.

questions.q: Which of these is a polyatomic ion?
questions.a: NH4+ (ammonium) is formed from atoms of two elements, nitrogen and hydrogen, so it is polyatomic. The others are monoatomic ions.

questions.q:
Match the ion in column I with its name in column II.
Column I: 1. Fe2+  2. Fe3+  3. Cu+  4. Cu2+
Column II: (p) ferric  (q) cupric  (r) ferrous  (s) cuprous
questions.a: 1-r, 2-p, 3-s, 4-q: Fe2+ is ferrous, Fe3+ is ferric, Cu+ is cuprous and Cu2+ is cupric (Table 9.1).

questions.q: What is an ionic bond? Name one ionic compound and the two ions it is made of.
questions.a: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions that holds them together. Example: sodium chloride, made of sodium ions (Na+) and chloride ions (Cl-).
s: Ionic bond: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
Example with its ions, such as sodium chloride from Na+ and Cl-

questions.q: Name the following ionic compounds: (a) CaO (b) MgS (c) KBr.
questions.a: (a) Calcium oxide (b) Magnesium sulfide (c) Potassium bromide. In each, the cation is named first and the simple anion ends in -ide.
s: (a) calcium oxide
(b) magnesium sulfide
(c) potassium bromide

questions.q: An aluminium atom has the configuration 2, 8, 3 and a fluorine atom has 2, 7. When they form an ionic compound, which statement is correct?
o: Each aluminium atom gives three electrons, and three fluoride ions combine with one aluminium ion
Each aluminium atom gains three electrons, and one fluoride ion combines with three aluminium ions
Each fluorine atom gives one electron, and one fluoride ion combines with one aluminium ion
Each aluminium atom gives three electrons, and one fluoride ion combines with one aluminium ion
questions.a: Each aluminium atom gives three electrons (becoming Al3+), each fluorine atom takes one (becoming F-), so three fluoride ions balance one aluminium ion.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Calcium oxide is named with the cation first, and the name of the anion ends in -ide.
Reason (R): The names of polyatomic ions always end in -ide.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: oxide is a simple anion, and simple anions end in -ide. Names of polyatomic ions generally do NOT end in -ide (for example sulfate, nitrate, carbonate).

questions.q: Aluminium (atomic number 13, configuration 2, 8, 3) combines with oxygen (atomic number 8, configuration 2, 6) to form an ionic compound. (a) How many electrons does each aluminium atom lose, and how many does each oxygen atom gain? (b) Write the symbol of each ion with its number of protons and electrons. (c) How many aluminium ions and oxide ions are needed so that the charges balance, and how many electrons are transferred in all? (d) Write the formula and name of the compound. (e) Both ions in the compound have the same electronic configuration. Write it, and name the noble gas whose atom has this configuration.
questions.a: (a) Each aluminium atom loses 3 electrons; each oxygen atom gains 2. (b) Al3+: 13 protons, 10 electrons; O2-: 8 protons, 10 electrons. (c) Two Al3+ give +6 and three O2- give -6, so 2 aluminium ions and 3 oxide ions; 6 electrons are transferred in all. (d) Al2O3, aluminium oxide. (e) Each ion has 10 electrons arranged 2, 8, the configuration of neon.
s: (a) Al loses 3, O gains 2
(b) Al3+ with 13 p and 10 e; O2- with 8 p and 10 e
(c) 2 Al3+ and 3 O2- balance +6 and -6; 6 electrons transferred
(d) Al2O3, aluminium oxide
(e) 2, 8 for both ions; same as neon

questions.q: Tanvi says, 'A sodium ion has the stable configuration 2, 8, the same as a neon atom, so a sodium ion and a neon atom are the same thing.' Is she right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that after losing its one valence electron, a sodium ion has 10 electrons arranged 2, 8, a stable octet like neon. But the two are not the same: Na+ has 11 protons and 10 electrons, so it carries a +1 charge, while a neon atom has 10 protons and 10 electrons and is neutral. The number of protons decides the element, so Na+ is still sodium.
s: Right part: Na+ has 10 electrons in a stable 2, 8 octet
Difference: Na+ has 11 protons and a +1 charge; neon has 10 protons and is neutral
Verdict: partly right; the proton number keeps it sodium

questions.q: A school chemistry club in Bhopal is making ion cards for a display on ionic bonding. Each card gives only the numbers of protons and electrons in one ion, and the club's chart lists the atomic numbers O = 8, F = 9, Mg = 12 and K = 19. Card P: 12 protons, 10 electrons. Card Q: 8 protons, 10 electrons. Card R: 19 protons, 18 electrons. Card S: 9 protons, 10 electrons. (a) Write the symbol and charge of the ion on each card. (b) Which cards show cations, and which show anions? (c) Name the compound formed by P with Q, and by R with S. (d) The club wants one more compound in which one cation is joined to two anions, using two of these cards. Which pair should they choose? Name the compound and justify your choice by balancing the charges.
questions.a: (a) P: Mg2+ (12 - 10 = +2); Q: O2- (8 - 10 = -2); R: K+ (+1); S: F- (-1). (b) P and R are cations (more protons than electrons); Q and S are anions. (c) P with Q: magnesium oxide; R with S: potassium fluoride. (d) P with S: one Mg2+ (+2) is balanced by two F- (-1 each), giving magnesium fluoride, MgF2. The other cation-anion pairs need one-to-one (MgO, KF) or two cations to one anion (K2O), so only P with S fits.
s: (a) Mg2+, O2-, K+ and F-
(b) P and R cations; Q and S anions
(c) magnesium oxide and potassium fluoride
(d) P with S: Mg2+ with two F- balances +2 and -2, magnesium fluoride; other pairs do not give 1:2

questions.q: Lithium forms the ion Li+ and oxygen forms O2-. What is the formula of lithium oxide by the criss-cross method?
questions.a: Li2O: the charge 2 of oxide goes to lithium and the charge 1 of lithium goes to oxygen (1 is not written), so two Li+ balance one O2-.

questions.q: Hydrogen has valency 1 and oxygen has valency 2. By crossing over the valencies, what is the formula of their covalent compound?
questions.a: H2O: the valency 2 of oxygen becomes the subscript of hydrogen, and the valency 1 of hydrogen is not written after oxygen.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about writing chemical formulae.
I. In the formula of an ionic compound, the symbol of the anion is written first.
II. In Al(OH)3, the bracket with subscript 3 shows three hydroxide ions bound to one aluminium ion.
III. If a valency becomes 1 after criss-crossing, it is not written in the formula.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: the symbol of the cation is written first, followed by the anion.

questions.q: A school science club in Indore prints formula cards for a display on baking soda, which is sodium hydrogencarbonate. They have three cations, Na+, Ca2+ and NH4+, and want each one paired with the hydrogencarbonate ion, HCO3-. (a) Write the formula of sodium hydrogencarbonate. (b) Write the formula of calcium hydrogencarbonate, and find the total number of atoms in one formula unit. (c) Write the formula of ammonium hydrogencarbonate and say whether it needs any bracket. (d) The printer has produced two cards, 'CaHCO32' and '(NH4)(HCO3)'. The club has money to reprint only one card now. Which card is more misleading and should be reprinted first? Justify using the bracket rule.
questions.a: (a) NaHCO3 (charges +1 and -1 balance one to one). (b) Ca(HCO3)2: one Ca2+ needs two HCO3- ions; atoms = 1 Ca + 2 H + 2 C + 6 O = 11. (c) NH4HCO3: one NH4+ balances one HCO3-, and brackets are not required when only one polyatomic ion of each type is present. (d) Reprint 'CaHCO32' first: without the bracket it reads as one Ca, one H, one C and 32 O atoms, hiding that there are two HCO3- ions; the bracket is needed when two or more polyatomic ions of the same type are present. '(NH4)(HCO3)' has unnecessary brackets but still shows the right ions in the right 1:1 ratio, so it is less misleading.
s: (a) NaHCO3
(b) Ca(HCO3)2 with 11 atoms per formula unit
(c) NH4HCO3, no bracket needed for single polyatomic ions
(d) reprint CaHCO32 first: it hides the two HCO3- ions; the other card only adds unneeded brackets

questions.q: True or False: 'The formula of ammonium chloride, made from NH4+ and Cl- ions, is NH4Cl, written without a bracket.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The charges +1 and -1 balance one to one, so there is only one ammonium ion in the formula, and brackets are used only when two or more polyatomic ions of the same type are present.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: one NH4+ balances one Cl-, and a single polyatomic ion needs no bracket

questions.q: A store-room label must show the formula of barium nitrate, made from Ba2+ and NO3- ions. Which formula should it carry?
questions.a: Ba(NO3)2: one Ba2+ needs two NO3- ions to balance its charge, and the nitrate is put in a bracket because two polyatomic ions of the same type are present.

questions.q:
Match each pair of ions (column I) with the number of oxygen atoms in one formula unit of the compound they form (column II).
Column I: 1. Ca2+ and OH-  2. Fe3+ and NO3-  3. Na+ and CO3 2-  4. Mg2+ and NO3-
Column II: (p) 3  (q) 6  (r) 2  (s) 9
questions.a: 1-r, 2-s, 3-p, 4-q: Ca(OH)2 has 2 oxygen atoms, Fe(NO3)3 has 3 x 3 = 9, Na2CO3 has 3, and Mg(NO3)2 has 2 x 3 = 6.

questions.q: (a) Write the formulae of cupric oxide (Cu2+ with O2-) and cuprous oxide (Cu+ with O2-) by the criss-cross method. (b) Why does cupric oxide need simplifying after criss-crossing while cuprous oxide does not?
questions.a: (a) Cupric oxide: CuO; cuprous oxide: Cu2O. (b) For Cu2+ and O2- criss-crossing gives Cu2O2, whose subscripts share the common factor 2, so it is divided to CuO. For Cu+ and O2- it gives Cu2O, where 2 and 1 have no common factor.
s: (a) CuO and Cu2O
(b) Cu2O2 has a common factor 2 and becomes CuO; Cu2O has none

questions.q: A metal M forms a sulfate with the formula MSO4 and a chloride with the formula MCl2. (a) Find the charge on the ion of M, showing how each formula tells you. (b) Predict the formula of the hydroxide of M. (c) Predict the formula of the nitrate of M.
questions.a: (a) SO4 has charge 2-, and one M balances one SO4 2- (after simplifying), so M carries 2+; in MCl2 one M balances two Cl- ions, which again gives 2+. (b) M2+ with OH- gives M(OH)2. (c) M2+ with NO3- gives M(NO3)2.
s: (a) M is M2+, shown by both MSO4 and MCl2
(b) M(OH)2
(c) M(NO3)2

questions.q: Write the chemical formula of each compound by the criss-cross method, using the ions given: (i) potassium sulfide from K+ and S2- (ii) calcium bromide from Ca2+ and Br- (iii) silver nitrate from Ag+ and NO3- (iv) ammonium carbonate from NH4+ and CO3 2-.
questions.a: (i) K2S (ii) CaBr2 (iii) AgNO3 (iv) (NH4)2CO3. In (iv) the ammonium ion is in a bracket because there are two NH4+ ions.
s: (i) K2S
(ii) CaBr2
(iii) AgNO3
(iv) (NH4)2CO3 with the bracket

questions.q: Naphthalene is a covalent compound. In Activity 9.4, it is most likely to dissolve in
o: kerosene and petrol, but not water
water, but not kerosene or petrol
none of water, kerosene and petrol
questions.a: Kerosene and petrol, but not water: most covalent compounds, such as camphor and naphthalene, are insoluble in water but dissolve in kerosene and petrol.

questions.q: Using N = 14 u and H = 1 u, what is the molecular mass of ammonia, NH3?

Assertion (A): Dry crystals of sodium chloride do not make the bulb glow in the conductivity set-up.
Reason (R): In the solid state, the ions of an ionic compound are held in fixed positions by strong forces.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: to conduct electricity the ions must be free to move, which they are not in the solid.

questions.q: Find the formula unit mass of (a) magnesium oxide, MgO, and (b) sodium sulfide, Na2S. Use Mg = 24 u, O = 16 u, Na = 23 u and S = 32 u.
s: (a) MgO = 40 u
(b) Na2S = 78 u

questions.q: Using H = 1 u, N = 14 u, O = 16 u, S = 32 u, Cl = 35.5 u, K = 39 u and Ca = 40 u, find the mass of each and say whether it is a molecular mass or a formula unit mass: (a) hydrogen chloride, HCl (b) sulfur dioxide, SO2 (c) ammonium chloride, NH4Cl (d) potassium oxide, K2O (e) calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2.
questions.a: (a) HCl = 1 + 35.5 = 36.5 u, molecular mass (covalent). (b) SO2 = 32 + (16 x 2) = 64 u, molecular mass (covalent). (c) NH4Cl = 14 + (1 x 4) + 35.5 = 53.5 u, formula unit mass (ionic: NH4+ and Cl-). (d) K2O = (39 x 2) + 16 = 94 u, formula unit mass (ionic). (e) Ca(OH)2 = 40 + (16 + 1) x 2 = 74 u, formula unit mass (ionic).
s: (a) HCl = 36.5 u, molecular mass
(b) SO2 = 64 u, molecular mass
(c) NH4Cl = 53.5 u, formula unit mass
(d) K2O = 94 u, formula unit mass
(e) Ca(OH)2 = 74 u, formula unit mass

questions.q: A student tests four unknown white solids as in Activity 9.4. Which single observation shows that a solid is most likely NOT an ionic compound?
o: It dissolves in petrol but not in water
It does not make the bulb glow as a dry solid
It has a high melting point
questions.a: It dissolves in petrol but not in water: ionic compounds are generally soluble in water and insoluble in petrol and kerosene. A dry ionic solid also fails to light the bulb, and ionic compounds dissolve in water and have high melting points, so those observations fit an ionic compound.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. Sugar dissolves in water, but its solution does not conduct electricity.
II. Ionic compounds generally have low melting and boiling points.
III. Taking C = 12 u and O = 16 u, the molecular mass of CO2 is 28 u.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only. Statement II is wrong: ionic compounds generally have HIGH melting and boiling points because of strong inter-ionic attractions. Statement III is wrong: CO2 = 12 + (16 x 2) = 44 u (28 u is the mass of CO).

questions.q: True or False: 'Using Ba = 137 u, O = 16 u and H = 1 u, the formula unit mass of barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)2, is 154 u.' Give the verdict and the correct working.
questions.a: False. The subscript 2 outside the bracket applies to the whole OH group: Ba(OH)2 = 137 + (16 + 1) x 2 = 137 + 34 = 171 u. The value 154 u counts only one OH.
s: Verdict: False
Correct working: 137 + (16 + 1) x 2 = 171 u, the bracket doubling the whole OH

questions.q: Aluminium sulfate has the formula Al2(SO4)3. Use Al = 27 u, S = 32 u and O = 16 u. (a) How many atoms of each element are there in one formula unit? (b) Find its formula unit mass. (c) A student writes 27 + 32 + (16 x 4) = 123 u. Point out his two mistakes. (d) Why is this value called a formula unit mass and not a molecular mass?
questions.a: (a) Al: 2, S: 3 (1 x 3), O: 12 (4 x 3). (b) (27 x 2) + {32 + (16 x 4)} x 3 = 54 + 96 x 3 = 54 + 288 = 342 u. (c) He took only one aluminium atom instead of two, and he did not multiply the SO4 group by the subscript 3 outside the bracket. (d) Aluminium sulfate is an ionic compound; its ions form a 3-D crystal and not molecules, so the mass is that of a formula unit, the simplest whole-number ratio of its ions.
s: (a) 2 Al, 3 S and 12 O atoms
(b) formula unit mass = 342 u
(c) used one Al instead of two, and ignored the 3 outside the bracket
(d) ionic compound forms crystals, not molecules, so it has a formula unit

questions.q: A grocery shop in Jaipur has two jars of white crystals whose labels have come off. One holds sugar (C12H22O11) and the other potassium chloride (KCl). The shopkeeper's daughter, a Class 9 student, tests them with a 9 V battery, a bulb and two electrodes. Jar A: dry crystals, bulb off; dissolved in water, bulb glows. Jar B: dry crystals, bulb off; dissolves in water, bulb stays off. (a) Which jar holds potassium chloride? Give a reason. (b) Using C = 12 u, H = 1 u, O = 16 u, K = 39 u and Cl = 35.5 u, find the molecular mass of sugar and the formula unit mass of potassium chloride. (c) Why did the dry crystals in Jar A not light the bulb? (d) Next month the battery is not working. Her brother says, 'Just dissolve a pinch of each in water; the one that dissolves is the salt.' Should she follow his test, or is another property from the chapter better? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Jar A: its water solution conducts, which shows free ions, so it is the ionic compound potassium chloride; sugar dissolves but gives no ions. (b) Sugar: (12 x 12) + (1 x 22) + (16 x 11) = 144 + 22 + 176 = 342 u. KCl: 39 + 35.5 = 74.5 u. (c) In the solid, the K+ and Cl- ions are held in fixed positions by strong forces and are not free to move, so no current flows. (d) His test will not work: both sugar and potassium chloride dissolve in water, as Jars A and B already showed. A better property is the melting point: ionic compounds generally have high melting points and covalent compounds usually low ones, so on gentle heating the sugar would melt and the potassium chloride would not. A kerosene or petrol test would not separate them either, because neither sugar nor potassium chloride dissolves in kerosene.
s: (a) Jar A is KCl: its solution conducts because it gives free ions
(b) sugar 342 u; KCl 74.5 u
(c) ions held in fixed positions in the solid, not free to move
(d) reject the water test (both dissolve; a kerosene test fails too); use melting point: sugar melts on gentle heating, KCl does not
